power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: We proposed knowing sufficiency as a psychological construct comprising knowing what and how much is sufficient for one's well-being, not seeking beyond that point, and feeling content with what is already present in one's life.

Existing psychological measures related to sufficiency primarily assess affective aspects such as dispositional contentment, but not the cognitive and behavioral aspects of recognizing what is enough and refraining from further pursuit.
We therefore developed and validated the Knowing Sufficiency Scale (KSS) to assess individual differences across these cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions among Japanese adults.
Following item generation and evaluation by experts and the target population, we collected two independent online survey samples, with final analytic sample sizes of n = 443 and n = 455.
We conducted exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and examined internal consistency, construct validity through correlations with related measures, and incremental validity.
A further assessment was conducted approximately 2 weeks later, with 294 participants included in the test-retest analysis.
The resulting KSS comprised 19 items across three subscales: Knowing What Is Enough, Stopping at Enough, and Felt Sufficiency.
A higher-order three-factor model showed acceptable fit on CFI, TLI, and SRMR, but not RMSEA, and fitted better than a one-factor model.
Cronbach's α and McDonald's ω in both samples and test-retest ICCs were all at least .70, indicating acceptable to good reliability.

The KSS overall and subscale scores generally showed positive associations with contentment, life satisfaction, savoring, gratitude, and psychological well-being, and negative associations with materialism, depressive symptoms, and ability-related social comparison orientation.
Adding Knowing What Is Enough and Stopping at Enough to a model including age, gender, savoring, and gratitude increased the explained variance in contentment by 7.55 percentage points.
The findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of the KSS.
The scale offers a means of studying knowing sufficiency in terms of its cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions.
Further research is needed to establish generalizability across languages and populations and to examine validity through associations with behavioral measures.
Materialism, which places material possessions and acquisition at the center of one's values and goals in life [1], is not necessarily associated with greater well-being.

text.text: The idea of knowing what is enough and stopping at that point has a long intellectual history.
In Chapter 44, the Dao De Jing, a foundational Daoist text, presents knowing contentment (知足) and knowing when to stop (知止) in parallel [4].

text.text: It frames them as practically important because excessive attachment and accumulation can lead to loss and harm, an emphasis on limits that resonates with contemporary sufficiency approaches to sustainability.
The Lotus Sutra, a major Mahayana Buddhist scripture, likewise identifies having few desires and being content with what one has (少欲知足) as a desirable quality of those who practice its teachings [5].

text.text: Taken together, these traditions motivated our focus on individual differences in how people recognize and respond to sufficiency in their lives.

Sufficiency at the individual level has been operationalized in terms of attitudes toward resource consumption and frugal living [6], as well as subjective sufficiency in income and material living conditions [7, 8].

text.text: However, these operationalizations focus on consumption and economic domains.
They therefore do not capture sufficiency as a broader psychological construct across life domains.
In psychology, contentment is a concept related to sufficiency.

Cordaro et al. [9] conceptualized contentment as an emotion that arises when one's present circumstances are appraised as whole and enough, a conceptualization subsequently examined empirically by Cordaro et al. [10].

text.text: These existing conceptualizations of dispositional contentment capture the affective experience of having enough, but do not directly assess the cognitive and behavioral aspects of sufficiency.
We therefore propose knowing sufficiency as a comprehensive psychological construct encompassing these cognitive, behavioral, and affective elements.
We define this construct as knowing what and how much is sufficient for one's well-being, not seeking beyond that point, and feeling content with what is already present in one's life.
In this definition, well-being is used broadly, without commitment to a specific theoretical model, to cover physical and psychological states, activities, relationships, and material conditions.
The term knowing refers not only to an explicit understanding of what is sufficient, but also to an experiential or practical sense of when enough has been reached.
We distinguish three interrelated dimensions of knowing sufficiency.
The first, Knowing What Is Enough, is the cognitive dimension of understanding what one needs for well-being and what and how much is enough for oneself.
The second, Stopping at Enough, is the behavioral dimension of not going beyond what one judges to be enough, whether by seeking more or by continuing an activity after reaching that point.
The third, Felt Sufficiency, is the affective dimension of experiencing a sense of sufficiency or contentment with what is already present in one's life.
Measuring these three dimensions separately may allow a more nuanced understanding of individual differences in knowing sufficiency.
This study aimed to develop and validate the Knowing Sufficiency Scale (KSS) as a measure of individual differences in this construct among Japanese adults.
Following item generation, we examined the relevance, comprehensiveness, and comprehensibility of the items through evaluations by experts and non-expert adults from the target population.

We first examined the scale's factor structure using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) in Sample 1, and then tested the three-factor structure of knowing sufficiency using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent Sample 2.
We also tested hypotheses concerning the construct validity of the KSS in each sample.
In Sample 1, incremental validity was examined by testing whether the KSS provided information about dispositional contentment beyond closely related measures of savoring and gratitude.
Finally, test-retest reliability over a 2week interval was assessed in Sample 2.
The hypotheses concerning construct validity are detailed in Supplementary Table S1.

text.text: First, we expected knowing sufficiency to show moderate-to-large positive correlations with dispositional contentment, dispositional joy, life satisfaction, savoring, and dispositional gratitude.
In particular, because Felt Sufficiency represents the affective dimension, we expected it to correlate more strongly with dispositional contentment than the other subscales.

We also expected a moderate negative correlation with the tendency to compare one's abilities with those of others, on the premise that people higher in knowing sufficiency are satisfied according to their own standards.
Self-acceptance, a dimension of psychological well-being, was expected to show a large positive correlation because it is conceptually similar.

In contrast, small-to-moderate correlations were expected with Personal Growth, Purpose in Life, Autonomy, and related dimensions, because achievement and growth were expected to be less important to people higher in knowing sufficiency.
Materialism was considered to contrast conceptually with knowing sufficiency and was therefore expected to show moderate-to-large negative correlations.
The cognitive dimension, Knowing What Is Enough, includes individual differences in how clearly people understand what would make them feel content.
Because this aspect partly overlaps with the emphasis on values clarification in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy [13], a moderate positive association with values was expected.
text.formatted: Because this aspect partly overlaps with the emphasis on values clarification in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, a moderate positive association with values was expected.

text.text: The behavioral dimension, Stopping at Enough, measures individual differences in the tendency to stop seeking more than is sufficient.
Because this involves refraining from further pursuit out of contentment rather than depression, we expected a small negative correlation with depressive symptoms.
We also expected a small negative correlation with the Behavioral Inhibition System (BIS), because Stopping at Enough does not entail refraining from pursuit out of fear of punishment.
Finally, because Stopping at Enough involves not seeking rewards or excitement excessively, small negative correlations with Behavioral Activation System (BAS) Drive and Fun Seeking were expected.
These hypotheses were tested to evaluate the construct validity of the KSS.

We examined a three-factor solution in light of both the factor-retention results and the theoretically proposed cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions.

For the 19 items selected in Sample 1, we examined a one-factor model in which all items loaded on a single factor and a higher-order three-factor model in which the cognitive, behavioral, and affective first-order factors loaded on a common higher-order factor.

Because the higher-order portion of a model with three first-order factors is just-identified and yields the same overall fit as a correlated three-factor model, the latter was not examined separately.
Items were treated as ordered categorical variables, and estimation used weighted least squares with mean and variance adjustment (WLSMV).

Model fit was evaluated using the mean-and varianceadjusted χ² statistic, comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) and its 95% confidence interval, and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR).

text.text: To examine incremental validity in Sample 1, we conducted a hierarchical multiple regression analysis with DPES Contentment as the dependent variable.
Step 1 included gender, age, the total savoring score, and gratitude as predictors.
Savoring and gratitude were selected because they were expected to be related to knowing sufficiency and to explain substantial variation in contentment.
Felt Sufficiency had considerable content overlap with DPES Contentment and was therefore considered unsuitable for examining the distinctive contribution of the KSS through incremental validity.
Accordingly, only the other two subscales, Knowing What Is Enough and Stopping at Enough, were entered at Step 2.
Regression coefficients were estimated using ordinary least squares.

Discussion In this study, we proposed knowing sufficiency as a psychological construct comprising knowing what and how much is sufficient for one's well-being, not seeking beyond that point, and feeling content with what is already present in one's life, and developed the KSS in Japanese adults.

Content validity assessment, addressing item relevance, comprehensiveness, and comprehensibility, and factor analyses in two independent samples yielded a 19-item scale comprising Knowing What Is Enough, Stopping at Enough, and Felt Sufficiency.
Internal consistency and approximately 2-week test-retest reliability coefficients met the specified criteria.

Correlations with related constructs were consistent with several hypotheses, and the cognitive and behavioral dimensions were associated with dispositional contentment after accounting for savoring and gratitude.
However, RMSEA did not meet the specified criterion for acceptable fit, and some correlations with related constructs did not meet our initial expectations.
These findings provide initial evidence concerning the measurement properties of the KSS while also indicating a need to refine the conceptual positioning of knowing sufficiency.
For the final 19 items, both parallel analysis and MAP in the EFA suggested three factors.
Each item loaded most strongly on its intended factor, and all loadings on other factors were below .30 in absolute value.
CFA in the independent Sample 2 indicated that the higher-order three-factor model fitted better than the one-factor model.
Although CFI, TLI, and SRMR met the guidelines specified in this study, RMSEA was .103 [95% CI: .096-.111], so not all indices indicated acceptable fit.
We cannot conclude that the current simple-structure model adequately accounts for the covariances among items.
Taken together, however, the findings provide some support for the structural validity of the KSS in distinguishing its three dimensions.
Regarding internal consistency, α and ω were at least .70 for the KSS overall score and each subscale in both samples.
Nevertheless, coefficients for Stopping at Enough were lower than those for the other two subscales.
This may partly reflect its smaller number of items and its coverage of behaviors across different contexts, including acquisition, continuation of activities, and eating.
For approximately 2-week test-retest reliability, ICC point estimates ranged from .720 to .791, indicating short-term stability of scores.

These findings are consistent with the purpose of the KSS as a measure of dispositional tendencies, although stability over longer intervals and the precision with which change can be measured require separate investigation.
The KSS was associated with dispositional contentment in the expected direction.

In particular, Felt Sufficiency showed a large correlation with DPES-J Contentment; its point estimate (r = .792) was larger than those for Knowing What Is Enough (r = .538) and Stopping at Enough (r = .423).
A similar pattern was observed for life satisfaction.
These findings are consistent with the interpretation of Felt Sufficiency as measuring the affective dimension of experiencing sufficiency in what one already has and in one's current life.
They also accord with the conceptualization of contentment as arising from appraising one's present circumstances as sufficient and complete [9, 10].
text.formatted: They also accord with the conceptualization of contentment as arising from appraising one's present circumstances as sufficient and complete <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: Associations with savoring were also consistent with the focus of knowing sufficiency on one's present life.
The KSS overall score showed a large positive correlation with Savoring the Moment and moderate positive correlations with Anticipating and Reminiscing.
Its positive association with gratitude further suggests that knowing sufficiency is related to savoring positive everyday experiences and positively appreciating what one already has.
However, the strength of these associations was not uniform: the correlation between Stopping at Enough and gratitude was smaller than the expected moderate association.
Conversely, correlations with Joy were larger than expected for the KSS overall score and Felt Sufficiency.
Thus, these associations may reflect not only a connection with contentment but also commonality with a broader range of positive emotions.
Associations with social comparison differed according to what was being compared.
As expected, the KSS overall score showed a moderate negative correlation with abilityrelated comparison (r = -.300).
However, it showed a moderate positive correlation with opinion-related comparison (r = .314), for which no hypothesis had been specified.
A broad interpretation that people higher in knowing sufficiency do not compare themselves with others therefore appears inappropriate.
Evaluating one's abilities in comparison with others needs to be distinguished from referring to others' opinions.
This distinction is consistent with the separation of ability and opinion comparison in the INCOM and its Japanese adaptation [26, 27].
text.formatted: This distinction is consistent with the separation of ability and opinion comparison in the INCOM and its Japanese adaptation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27]</ref>.

text.text: Knowing what is enough for oneself and being satisfied with one's present life may not imply a lack of interest in other people's perspectives.
Associations with psychological well-being revealed differences among the subscales in their relationships with Self-Acceptance.

Felt Sufficiency showed the expected large positive correlation with Self-Acceptance (r = .554), whereas the correlation for Stopping at Enough was small (r = .201), leaving some hypotheses unsupported.
An association between contentment and self-acceptance has also been reported previously [10, 12].
text.formatted: An association between contentment and self-acceptance has also been reported previously <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that this association may correspond relatively closely to the affective dimension of The associations with materialism were negative, as expected, but smaller in magnitude than anticipated.

Correlations of the KSS overall score with J-MVS-P6 Success/Centrality and Happiness were -.218 and -.342, respectively, and the expected moderate or large negative associations were generally not observed for the subscales either.
These findings do not support positioning knowing sufficiency as simply the opposite of materialism.
One possible explanation is that the KSS assesses not only material possessions but also physical and mental states, activities, and relationships, which may attenuate these associations.
Future research should therefore examine associations with actual ownership and acquisition behavior.
Regarding values, Knowing What Is Enough showed the expected moderate positive correlation with VQ Progress (r = .484).
VQ Progress assesses progress in valued living [13], suggesting an association between knowing what is enough for oneself and living in personally important directions.
text.formatted: VQ Progress assesses progress in valued living <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, suggesting an association between knowing what is enough for oneself and living in personally important directions.

text.text: However, the positive correlation between Felt Sufficiency and VQ Progress was larger than expected (r = .574).
Associations with valued living are therefore not limited to the cognitive dimension of knowing sufficiency.
The sense that one is living in accordance with what matters personally may be closely related to the affective experience of contentment with one's present life.
Associations with BAS Drive differed from expectations for the KSS overall score and all three subscales.
We had expected no association or small negative associations with the KSS overall score, Knowing What Is Enough, and Felt Sufficiency, but instead observed small or moderate positive correlations.
In particular, the correlation with Knowing What Is Enough was r = .349.
The correlation with Stopping at Enough was close to zero (r = .033, 95% CI [-.059, .124]), so the expected negative association was not observed for this subscale either.
These findings suggest that higher knowing sufficiency should not be understood as weaker motivation to pursue goals.
Understanding what is enough for oneself may be compatible with actively pursuing what one considers necessary.
In contrast, Stopping at Enough showed a small negative correlation with BAS Fun Seeking (r = -.198), supporting the corresponding hypothesis.
It also showed the expected small negative correlations with depressive symptoms and BIS (r = -.189 and -.195, respectively).
This pattern supports the possibility that being able to stop at sufficiency differs from refraining from pursuit simply because one is depressed or because of sensitivity to punishment.

In the hierarchical multiple regression analysis, adding Knowing What Is Enough and Stopping at Enough to a model containing age, gender, savoring, and gratitude increased the explained variance in DPES-J Contentment by 7.55 percentage points.
Both added subscales were positively associated with contentment after accounting for the other variables.

Beyond savoring positive experiences and feeling grateful, knowing what is enough for oneself and tending to stop further pursuit once sufficiency is reached therefore provided additional information for understanding individual differences in dispositional contentment.
These findings suggest that Knowing What Is Enough and Stopping at Enough have distinctive contributions to make as additional traits to consider in contentment research.

Taken together, this study highlights the value of examining knowing sufficiency in terms of recognizing what is enough, not seeking beyond that point, and experiencing contentment, rather than simply as low materialism or weak motivation to pursue things.
In particular, its positive associations with goal pursuit and valued living suggest that being content with what is already present may be compatible with engaging in meaningful activities.

Future research could measure the point at which individuals judge that they have enough and the point at which they actually stop an activity, for example in shopping or leisure contexts, and examine how these points relate to each KSS dimension.

Repeated assessments in daily life could also examine whether recognizing sufficiency precedes a reduction in further pursuit and feelings of contentment, or whether contentment curbs subsequent pursuit.
Such research could extend our understanding beyond correlations among individual differences in the three dimensions to the psychological processes linking them.

Replication incorporating Fourth, the KSS was developed in Japanese, and its measurement properties were examined in Japanese adults; its properties in other languages and populations remain unknown.

The English translations presented in this article are intended to communicate the item content, and their comprehensibility, factor structure, reliability, and validity have not been examined in English-speaking populations.
Use in other languages and cultures requires not only translation and content validity assessment but also further validation, including examination of measurement invariance.

This study developed the 19-item KSS to measure the cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions of knowing sufficiency and provided initial evidence for its factor structure, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity in Japanese adults.

In particular, the incremental validity of Knowing What Is Enough and Stopping at Enough for dispositional contentment suggests the value of measuring the cognitive and behavioral dimensions of knowing sufficiency to understand individual differences in contentment.
Nevertheless, questions remain regarding generalizability and some of the hypotheses.

text.text: We also did not test whether the association between knowing sufficiency and well-being remained after accounting for income and living conditions.
Including living conditions in future research will be important for distinguishing an actual lack of necessary resources from difficulty experiencing sufficiency despite having resources.
Second, the examinations of construct and incremental validity were based on associations among self-report measures administered at the same time.
Shared response tendencies [50] and overlapping item content may therefore have contributed to the associations, and neither causality nor its direction can be determined.

text.text: Although Stopping at Enough was designed to assess a behavioral dimension, it measured self-perceptions of behavior rather than actual behavior.
Further clarification of KSS validity requires the integration of behavioral indicators and assessments in daily life.
Third, the factor structure and item composition warrant further examination.
Fixing the small cross-loadings observed for several items in EFA to zero may have contributed to the inadequate RMSEA in CFA [51].
text.formatted: Fixing the small cross-loadings observed for several items in EFA to zero may have contributed to the inadequate RMSEA in CFA <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref>.

text.text: In Sample 2, we examined only conventional CFA models with cross-loadings fixed to zero and did not evaluate more flexible approaches such as exploratory structural equation modeling.
Future research using an independent sample may therefore need to refine the item composition or factor model.

In addition, content evaluations by experts and members of the target population were conducted mainly before item selection; the extent to which the final 19 items adequately cover the construct should be reassessed.
Item 12, "I can stop eating when I feel about 80% full," had a relatively low loading and communality in the final EFA.

Further examination of the behavioral items should consider both the benefit of including concrete everyday situations and the possibility that such items reflect domain-specific individual differences.

Associations with Purpose in Life were stronger than initially expected: the KSS overall score, Knowing What Is Enough, and Felt Sufficiency showed moderate positive correlations with this dimension.
Associations with Personal Growth were also positive.
Consistent with this pattern, Cordaro et al. [10] also reported positive associations of dispositional contentment with Purpose in Life and Personal Growth.
These findings are inconsistent with equating knowing sufficiency with a lack of purpose or growth.
Being content with what is already present in one's life may not necessarily conflict with having a sense of direction and experiencing personal growth.

The KSS provides a starting point for examining individual differences in knowing sufficiency across its cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions: knowing what and how much is sufficient for one's well-being, not seeking beyond that point, and feeling content with what is already present in one's life.

自分は何があれば満足に暮らせるかをわかっている I know what I need in order to live a satisfying life.
自分が心身ともに良い状態でいるのに必要な条件がわかっている I know what I need to stay mentally and physically well.
「自分はこれをすれば穏やかな満足感を感じられる」という決まった習慣がある I have a habit that I know brings me a sense of quiet contentment.
自分の幸せに必要なものと、なくてもいいものを区別できる I can distinguish between what I need for my happiness and what I can do without.
自分にとって何が過剰、あるいはやりすぎか、体感としてわかる I can sense what is excessive for me or when I am overdoing something.
何をどれだけ求めれば十分か、自分なりの基準を持っている I have my own standards for what to seek and how much is enough.
自分にとっての「これで十分」がどのあたりか、感覚的にわかる I have an intuitive sense of what counts as "enough" for me.
Stopping at Enough (Behavioral Subscale) 欲しいものでも、十分な量以上は求めない Even when I want something, I do not seek more of it once I have enough.
すでに足りているときには、さらに増やそうとしない When I already have enough, I do not try to get more.
好きなことでも、やりすぎないところで切り上げるようにしている Even when I am doing something I enjoy, I tend to stop before I overdo it.
欲しいものに執着しすぎる自分に気づいて立ち止まることができる I can notice when I am becoming too attached to something I want and then pause.
腹八分目で食事を終えることができる I can stop eating when I feel about 80% full.
今持っているもので十分だと感じることが多い I often feel that what I have now is enough.
自分の人生に必要なものは既にそろっていると気づく瞬間がある There are moments when I realize that I already have what I need in my life.
当たり前の日常に幸せを感じることが多い I often find happiness in the ordinary moments of everyday life.
日々の暮らしで「ちょうど良さ」を感じられる In my everyday life, I can feel that things are "just right."
たとえ多くを持っていなくても、今あるもので満足することができる Even if I do not have much, I can be content with what I have.
身近にあるものや人との関わりの中で満足できる I can find contentment in the things around me and in my interactions with others.
